topics.title: Present perfect vs past simple
topics.summary: The single most common tense mistake in English. Both talk about the past; the difference is whether the period is finished.
points: Past simple: the time is finished and usually stated — yesterday, last year, in 2019.
Present perfect: the period runs up to now, or the result still matters — ever, never, since, for, this week.
Never put present perfect with a finished time. "I have seen it yesterday" is always wrong.
"Since" takes a point in time; "for" takes a length of time.

questions.prompt: I ___ in Manchester since I was a child.
questions.explanation: "Since I was a child" runs from the past up to now, which is the present perfect. "Lived" would suggest you no longer live there.

questions.prompt: She ___ her keys this morning, but she found them again.
questions.explanation: "This morning" is finished — it is now later in the day and the keys were found — so past simple. If it were still morning, "has lost" would work.

questions.prompt: ___ you ever ___ sushi?
questions.explanation: "Ever" means at any time up to now, so present perfect: have + past participle. "Ate" is the past simple form and cannot follow "have".

questions.prompt: We ___ to Japan three times.
questions.explanation: Counting experiences up to now takes present perfect. Use "have been" for visits you have returned from; "have gone" means still away.

questions.prompt: He ___ that film last night and hated it.
questions.explanation: "Last night" is a finished time expression, so it takes past simple. This is the pairing to check first whenever you are unsure.

questions.prompt: I've worked here ___ eight years.
questions.explanation: Eight years is a length of time, so "for". "Since" would need a starting point: since 2018.

questions.prompt: Sorry about the mess — I ___ the kitchen.
questions.explanation: The present perfect continuous explains a present situation by the recent activity behind it. The mess is the visible result of the painting.

questions.prompt: When ___ you ___ your driving test?
questions.explanation: A "when" question asks for a specific finished time, so past simple. English never uses "when" with the present perfect in this way.

questions.prompt: She ___ that film three times, and she still cries at the end.
questions.explanation: The three viewings are counted up to now, and she still reacts now, so the time frame is unfinished. Present perfect. "Saw" would close the story off in the past.

questions.prompt: ___ you ever ___ to an interview in another language?
questions.explanation: "Ever" asks about any time in your life so far, which is present perfect. "Been" means you went and came back; "gone" would mean you are still there.

questions.prompt: I ___ my keys, so I cannot get in.
questions.explanation: The losing happened in the past but the result — being locked out — is happening now. When the present result is the point, use present perfect.

questions.prompt: We ___ in this flat for two years before we bought the house.
questions.explanation: Two past events: living, then buying. Past perfect marks the one that came first. Present perfect cannot be used, because "before we bought" closes the time frame.

questions.prompt: He ___ his homework yet.
questions.explanation: "Yet" means up to this moment, so the time frame reaches the present. It pairs with present perfect, not past simple.

questions.prompt: They ___ the results last Friday.
questions.explanation: "Last Friday" is a finished time, and a finished time takes past simple. This is the commonest present-perfect error: a specific past date rules it out.

questions.prompt: How long ___ you ___ for this company?
questions.explanation: "How long" about a job you still have runs from the past to now, so present perfect. Past simple would suggest you have left.

questions.prompt: I ___ never ___ such a crowded station.
questions.explanation: "Never" here means at no point in my life up to now, which is present perfect. Note the past participle "seen", not "saw".

topics.title: a, an, the — and no article
topics.summary: Articles are tiny and carry almost no meaning, which is exactly why they are hard: there is nothing to hear. They are also the most common error in IELTS writing.
points: "a"/"an" introduces something for the first time, or says what kind of thing it is.
"the" points at something both people already know about — mentioned before, or unique.
Use no article for general statements with plurals and uncountables: "Dogs bark", "Water is wet".
"an" goes before a vowel *sound*, not a vowel letter: an hour, a university.

questions.prompt: I bought ___ book yesterday. ___ book was about volcanoes.
questions.explanation: First mention takes "a" because the listener does not know which book yet. Once mentioned, it becomes known, so the second takes "the".

questions.prompt: ___ children need plenty of sleep.
questions.explanation: This is a general statement about children everywhere, so a plural noun takes no article. "The children" would mean particular ones.

questions.prompt: She waited for ___ hour.
questions.explanation: "Hour" begins with a vowel sound, since the h is silent, so it takes "an". Compare "a university", where the u sounds like "yoo".

questions.prompt: ___ sun rose at six.
questions.explanation: There is only one sun, so it is automatically known and takes "the". The same goes for the moon, the sky and the sea.

questions.prompt: My brother is ___ engineer.
questions.explanation: Jobs take a/an in English, and "engineer" starts with a vowel sound, so "an". Leaving it out is a very common error.

questions.prompt: We went to ___ cinema on Saturday.
questions.explanation: Places like the cinema, the theatre and the bank take "the" even on first mention, because the speaker means the usual one.

questions.prompt: ___ information in this report is out of date.
questions.explanation: "In this report" identifies exactly which information, so "the". Note "information" is uncountable and can never take "a".

questions.prompt: He plays ___ guitar and studies ___ history.
questions.explanation: Musical instruments take "the" after "play"; school subjects take no article. Both are fixed patterns worth memorising as a pair.

questions.prompt: She works as ___ engineer at ___ university near here.
questions.explanation: "Engineer" starts with a vowel sound, so "an". "University" starts with a "y" sound, so "a" — the rule follows the sound, not the letter.

questions.prompt: Could you pass me ___ salt, please?
questions.explanation: There is one salt on the table and you both know which. "The" is for something already identified by the situation.

questions.prompt: ___ honest answer is worth more than a clever one.
questions.explanation: "Honest" begins with a silent h, so the first sound is a vowel and the article is "an".

questions.prompt: I love ___ music, especially ___ music my grandmother played.
questions.explanation: Music in general takes no article. The second one is a specific music, defined by the clause after it, so it takes "the".

questions.prompt: We flew over ___ Alps on the way to ___ Italy.
questions.explanation: Mountain ranges take "the"; most countries take no article. "The Netherlands" and "the United States" are exceptions because they are plural or descriptive.

questions.prompt: He is ___ best candidate we have interviewed.
questions.explanation: Superlatives point to one thing only, so they take "the". There cannot be two bests.

questions.prompt: She goes to ___ school by bus, and her mother works at ___ school.
questions.explanation: Going to school as a pupil is the institution, so no article. Her mother works at a building, a specific one, so "the".

questions.prompt: There is ___ hour left before ___ train leaves.
questions.explanation: "Hour" begins with a silent h, so "an". The train is a particular one you are both waiting for, so "the".

topics.title: The three conditionals
topics.summary: Conditionals are just an if-clause plus a result clause. What changes is how real the situation is, and each level has a fixed pair of tenses.
points: First: if + present simple, will + verb. A real future possibility.
Second: if + past simple, would + verb. Imagined or unlikely, now or in the future.
Third: if + past perfect, would have + past participle. A past that did not happen.
Never put "will" or "would" inside the if-clause.

questions.prompt: If it ___ tomorrow, we'll stay in.
questions.explanation: First conditional: the if-clause takes the present simple even though it refers to the future. "Will" belongs only in the result clause.

questions.prompt: If I ___ rich, I would buy a boat.
questions.explanation: Second conditional for an imagined present. Formal English uses "were" for every subject here — "if I were you" is the everyday example.

questions.prompt: If she had left earlier, she ___ the train.
questions.explanation: Third conditional: "had left" pairs with "would have caught". The situation is over and cannot be changed.

questions.prompt: I'd help you if I ___ time.
questions.explanation: Second conditional. The past simple "had" signals that this is unreal — the speaker does not have time.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: If you will come early, we can talk.
If you come early, we can talk.
If you would come early, we can talk.
If you came early, we will talk.
questions.explanation: "Will" and "would" never go inside the if-clause. Option 4 mixes a second-conditional if-clause with a first-conditional result.

questions.prompt: If we ___ the map, we wouldn't be lost now.
questions.explanation: A mixed conditional: a past cause ("had brought") with a present result ("wouldn't be"). These are common and worth recognising.

questions.prompt: Water ___ if you heat it to 100°C.
questions.explanation: The zero conditional: present simple in both halves, for something always true. Facts and scientific results take this form.

questions.prompt: ___ I known, I would have said something.
questions.explanation: A formal third conditional can drop "if" and invert instead: "Had I known" means "If I had known". This scores well in writing.

questions.prompt: If it ___ tomorrow, we will move the picnic indoors.
questions.explanation: First conditional: present simple after "if", "will" in the other half. "Will" never follows "if" in this pattern.

questions.prompt: If I ___ you, I would take the earlier flight.
questions.explanation: Second conditional advice uses "were" for every person. "If I was" is heard in speech but is marked wrong in writing.

questions.prompt: If she had revised, she ___ the exam.
questions.explanation: Third conditional, about an unchangeable past: "had" + past participle in one half, "would have" + past participle in the other.

questions.prompt: We would have arrived on time if the train ___ cancelled.
questions.explanation: The "if" half of a third conditional takes past perfect: "had not been".

questions.prompt: If you heat water to 100°C, it ___.
questions.explanation: This is the zero conditional — a fact that is always true. Both halves take present simple. "Will boil" would make it a prediction about one occasion.

questions.prompt: If I had studied medicine, I ___ a doctor now.
questions.explanation: A mixed conditional: the condition is past but the result is present, so "had studied" pairs with "would be" rather than "would have been".

questions.prompt: ___ you need anything, just ring the bell.
questions.explanation: "Should you need" is a formal inversion of "if you need". The "if" is dropped and "should" moves to the front.

questions.prompt: She would travel more if she ___ so much annual leave.
questions.explanation: Second conditional about now: past simple in the "if" half, even though the meaning is present.

topics.title: Verb + -ing or verb + to
topics.summary: Some verbs must be followed by -ing, others by "to". There is no rule that predicts which — but there are reliable groups, and a few verbs change meaning.
points: -ing after: enjoy, avoid, deny, suggest, consider, risk, finish, mind, practise.
"to" after: want, decide, hope, promise, agree, offer, refuse, manage, afford.
After a preposition, always -ing: good at swimming, instead of waiting.
"Stop", "remember" and "try" change meaning depending on which you use.

questions.prompt: He denied ___ the window.
questions.explanation: "Deny" always takes -ing. So do admit, avoid, suggest and consider — the group is worth learning together.

questions.prompt: They agreed ___ the price.
questions.explanation: "Agree" takes the to-infinitive, like decide, hope, promise and refuse.

questions.prompt: I'm not very good at ___ decisions.
questions.explanation: "At" is a preposition, and a verb after a preposition is always -ing. This rule has no exceptions, which makes it worth trusting.

questions.prompt: We stopped ___ petrol on the way.
questions.explanation: "Stop to do" means pause in order to do it; "stop doing" means end the activity. Here they stopped the car in order to buy petrol.

questions.prompt: Would you mind ___ the door?
questions.explanation: "Mind" takes -ing. "Would you mind closing…" is one of the most useful polite request forms in English.

questions.prompt: She managed ___ the deadline despite everything.
questions.explanation: "Manage to" means succeeded in doing something difficult, and always takes the to-infinitive.

questions.prompt: Remember ___ the oven off before you leave.
questions.explanation: "Remember to do" is about a future duty; "remember doing" is about a past memory. Here it is an instruction, so the infinitive.

questions.prompt: The council is considering ___ the library.
questions.explanation: "Consider" takes -ing. A useful test: if you can put "the idea of" in front, the verb needs -ing.

questions.prompt: I cannot afford ___ a new laptop this year.
questions.explanation: "Afford" is always followed by the infinitive with "to".

questions.prompt: Would you mind ___ the window?
questions.explanation: "Mind" takes the -ing form. The polite request is literally asking whether the opening would bother you.

questions.prompt: He stopped ___ because the doctor told him to.
questions.explanation: "Stop" + -ing means you ended the activity. "Stop to smoke" would mean you paused something else in order to have a cigarette.

questions.prompt: She promised ___ me as soon as she landed.
questions.explanation: "Promise" takes the infinitive with "to".

questions.prompt: I remember ___ the door, but now I am not sure.
questions.explanation: "Remember" + -ing is a memory of something already done. "Remember to lock" would be a reminder about the future.

questions.prompt: They suggested ___ the meeting until Monday.
questions.explanation: "Suggest" never takes "to" + infinitive. Use the -ing form, or "suggest that we postpone".

questions.prompt: He let me ___ his notes before the exam.
questions.explanation: "Let" takes the bare infinitive — no "to". Compare "allow me to borrow", which does take "to".

questions.prompt: We look forward to ___ from you.
questions.explanation: The "to" in "look forward to" is a preposition, not part of an infinitive, so the -ing form follows it.

topics.title: The passive voice
topics.summary: The passive moves the thing affected to the front. Academic and report writing uses it constantly, because the process matters more than who did it.
points: Form: the right tense of "be" plus the past participle.
Use it when the doer is unknown, obvious, or simply not the point.
Add "by" only when the doer is genuinely worth naming.
Do not overuse it — a whole essay in the passive reads as evasive.

questions.prompt: The results ___ next week.
questions.explanation: The results do not announce themselves — someone announces them — so the passive is needed: will be + past participle.

questions.prompt: This bridge ___ in 1890.
questions.explanation: Past passive: was + built. The builder is unknown and unimportant, which is exactly when the passive earns its place.

questions.prompt: The report ___ by the committee at the moment.
questions.explanation: An action in progress takes the present continuous passive: is being + past participle.

questions.prompt: Change to the passive: "Someone has stolen my bike."
options: My bike was stolen by someone.
questions.explanation: Present perfect passive: has been + past participle. "By someone" is dropped because it adds nothing.

questions.prompt: The samples ___ before the test began.
questions.explanation: The preparation happened before another past event, so past perfect passive: had been + past participle.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the passive best?
options: The soup was eaten by me.
Mistakes were made in the calculation.
The ball was thrown by the boy.
The letter was written by me yesterday.
questions.explanation: The passive is right when the doer is unknown or beside the point. The other three name an obvious doer, so the active would be clearer.

questions.prompt: English ___ in over fifty countries.
questions.explanation: A general truth about how English is used takes the present simple passive: is + spoken.

questions.prompt: The proposal is expected ___ next month.
questions.explanation: The proposal receives the approval, so a passive infinitive is needed: to be + past participle.

questions.prompt: The bridge ___ in 1890 and is still in use.
questions.explanation: The bridge did not do the building, so the verb is passive: "was" + past participle.

questions.prompt: Your application ___ at the moment.
questions.explanation: An action in progress and done to the subject needs the present continuous passive: "is being" + past participle.

questions.prompt: The results ___ by the end of the week.
questions.explanation: The results receive the action, so the future passive is "will be" + past participle.

questions.prompt: This road ___ since March.
questions.explanation: "Since March" needs a present perfect, and the road receives the action, so present perfect passive: "has been" + past participle.

questions.prompt: The parcel ___ to the wrong address yesterday.
questions.explanation: Past simple passive. "Delivered" alone would mean the parcel did the delivering.

questions.prompt: Nothing ___ about the delay so far.
questions.explanation: "So far" reaches the present, and "nothing" receives the action, so present perfect passive.

questions.prompt: The windows need ___.
questions.explanation: "Need" + -ing has a passive meaning in English: the windows need to be cleaned. "Need to clean" would mean the windows do the cleaning.

questions.prompt: She ___ a scholarship by the university.
questions.explanation: With two objects, either can become the subject. Here she receives the award, so the passive is "was awarded".

topics.title: Relative clauses
topics.summary: Relative clauses let you add information without starting a new sentence. They are the fastest way to make writing sound less choppy — and to raise a grammar band.
points: who for people, which for things, that for either, whose for possession.
Defining clause (no commas): tells you which one, and cannot be removed.
Non-defining clause (commas): extra information you could delete. Never use "that" here.
Drop the pronoun only when it is the object: "the book (that) I read".

questions.prompt: The woman ___ car was stolen has called the police.
questions.explanation: The car belongs to the woman, so this is possession: "whose". Note it can be followed directly by a noun, unlike "who".

questions.prompt: My laptop, ___ I bought last year, has stopped working.
questions.explanation: The commas make this non-defining, and "that" is never allowed in a non-defining clause. "What" is not a relative pronoun here at all.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The students, who failed, must resit.
The students who failed must resit.
The students who failed, must resit.
The students, who failed must resit.
questions.explanation: Without commas it means only the students who failed. With commas it would mean all the students failed — a real change of meaning.

questions.prompt: That's the café ___ we first met.
questions.explanation: "Where" replaces "in which" for places. You could also say "the café that we first met in".

questions.prompt: In which sentence can the pronoun be left out?
options: The man who called was rude.
The film that we watched was long.
The road which leads north is closed.
The chef whose menu won is retiring.
questions.explanation: "We watched the film" — the pronoun is the object, so it can go: "The film we watched was long." In the others it is the subject and must stay.

questions.prompt: He missed the train, ___ made him late.
questions.explanation: "Which" here refers back to the whole preceding idea, not to a single noun. This use always needs a comma before it.

questions.prompt: The report, ___ was published in May, has been withdrawn.
questions.explanation: Non-defining clause about a thing, so "which". The commas tell you the clause could be removed and the sentence would still stand.

questions.prompt: Everything ___ he said turned out to be true.
questions.explanation: After "everything", "all" and "something", English prefers "that" and avoids "which". "What" would be wrong because "everything" is already there.

questions.prompt: The woman ___ car was stolen has reported it.
questions.explanation: "Whose" shows possession — the car belongs to the woman. "Who's" is a different word meaning "who is".

questions.prompt: The report, ___ was published in June, has been withdrawn.
questions.explanation: A clause between commas is non-defining — extra information — and non-defining clauses never take "that". Use "which".

questions.prompt: This is the café ___ we first met.
questions.explanation: The clause says the place of the meeting, so use "where". "Which we first met" would need "in" as well.

questions.prompt: The book ___ I lent you is overdue.
questions.explanation: "Which" (or "that") refers to things. "What" cannot introduce a relative clause after a noun.

questions.prompt: My brother, ___ lives in Perth, is visiting next month.
questions.explanation: Non-defining clause about a person: "who", never "that". The commas signal that you already know which brother.

questions.prompt: The year ___ she graduated was 2016.
questions.explanation: "When" is the relative adverb for time, in the same way "where" works for place.

questions.prompt: She is the colleague to ___ I sent the file.
questions.explanation: After a preposition the object form "whom" is required. In everyday speech you would move the preposition: "who I sent the file to".

questions.prompt: Everything ___ he said turned out to be true.
questions.explanation: After "everything", "all" and "nothing", English uses "that" rather than "which".

topics.title: Modal verbs: certainty and obligation
topics.summary: Modals are how English expresses how sure you are and how strong a rule is. Choosing the wrong one changes your meaning far more than a tense error would.
points: Certainty: must (sure it is true) → might/could (possible) → can't (sure it is not).
Obligation: must / have to (necessary) → should (advice) → needn't (not necessary).
"Mustn't" means it is forbidden. "Don't have to" means it is optional. They are opposites.
For the past, add "have" + past participle: must have been, should have gone.

questions.prompt: The lights are off — they ___ be out.
questions.explanation: "Must" expresses a confident conclusion from evidence. The dark house is the evidence, so the speaker is nearly certain.

questions.prompt: You ___ take photographs in the gallery — it's forbidden.
questions.explanation: "Mustn't" is a prohibition. "Don't have to" would mean photographs are optional, which is the opposite of what is meant.

questions.prompt: You ___ pay now; you can pay on the day.
questions.explanation: The second half says paying now is optional, which is "don't have to". "Mustn't" would forbid paying altogether.

questions.prompt: She's not answering. She ___ be in a meeting.
questions.explanation: "Might" marks a possible explanation rather than a certain one. "Must" would claim more than the evidence supports.

questions.prompt: That ___ be Tom — he's abroad this week.
questions.explanation: "Can't" is the negative of certainty: the speaker is sure it is not Tom. "Mustn't" is about rules, never about deduction.

questions.prompt: I ___ have left my umbrella on the bus.
questions.explanation: "Must have" + past participle is a confident conclusion about the past — the only place the umbrella could be.

questions.prompt: You ___ have told me — I'd have helped.
questions.explanation: "Should have" + past participle criticises a past action that did not happen. It is the standard way to express regret or reproach.

questions.prompt: Applicants ___ submit two references.
questions.explanation: "Must" states a requirement, which is the right register for a formal rule or instruction.

questions.prompt: You ___ be tired after that flight.
questions.explanation: "Must" here is a confident deduction, not an obligation — the speaker is sure, based on the evidence of a long flight.

questions.prompt: You ___ have told me earlier; I could have helped.
questions.explanation: "Should have" + past participle criticises something that did not happen but ought to have.

questions.prompt: She ___ be at home — I saw her at the office ten minutes ago.
questions.explanation: For a confident negative deduction English uses "cannot", not "must not". "Must not" is a prohibition.

questions.prompt: Applicants ___ submit two references.
questions.explanation: "Must" states a requirement of the process. "Can" would make it optional.

questions.prompt: ___ I open the window? It is rather warm.
questions.explanation: "Shall I" offers to do something. "Will I" is not used for offers in standard British usage.

questions.prompt: He ___ have missed the train — he left an hour early.
questions.explanation: Leaving early makes missing the train nearly impossible, so the confident negative deduction is "cannot have".

questions.prompt: You ___ pay now; the invoice is due next month.
questions.explanation: "Need not" means it is not necessary. "Must not" would forbid paying, which is not the meaning.

questions.prompt: It ___ rain later, so take an umbrella just in case.
questions.explanation: "Might" expresses possibility. "Must" would claim certainty, which "just in case" contradicts.

topics.title: Word order and inversion
topics.summary: English word order is fixed, which is why breaking it deliberately is so noticeable. Controlled inversion is one of the clearest signals of an advanced writer.
points: Normal order: subject, verb, object, then manner, place, time.
Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb but after "be": "She often walks", "She is often late".
A negative or restrictive adverb at the front forces inversion: never, seldom, rarely, not until, little.
"Hardly … when" and "no sooner … than" are fixed pairs; mixing them is a common error.

questions.prompt: Never ___ such a mess.
questions.explanation: A negative adverb in front position inverts the subject and auxiliary: "have I seen". Without the fronted "never", normal order returns.

questions.prompt: Which sentence has correct word order?
questions.explanation: An adverb of manner never separates the verb from its object. Say what she speaks first, then how.

questions.prompt: Not until the letter arrived ___ the truth.
questions.explanation: "Not until" triggers inversion in the *main* clause, not in the time clause. With no other auxiliary present, English supplies "did".

questions.prompt: He ___ late for work.
questions.explanation: Frequency adverbs come after "be" but before other main verbs. Compare "He never arrives late".

questions.prompt: No sooner had we sat down ___ the phone rang.
questions.explanation: "No sooner … than" is fixed. "Hardly … when" is the other fixed pair, and mixing the two is one of the most common advanced errors.

questions.prompt: Which is the natural order?
options: I went by train to Rome last week.
I went last week to Rome by train.
I went to Rome by train last week.
Last week to Rome I went by train.
questions.explanation: English prefers manner, place, then time — but place before manner sounds natural with "go to". Time reliably comes last.

questions.prompt: Only after the meeting ___ what had been decided.
questions.explanation: "Only after…" is restrictive, so the main clause inverts. The pattern is the same as "not until".

questions.prompt: So convincing ___ that nobody objected.
questions.explanation: "So + adjective" in front position inverts what follows. It is a strong, formal way to emphasise a quality.

questions.prompt: Never ___ such a generous offer.
questions.explanation: A negative adverb at the front forces inversion: auxiliary before subject. The verb after it stays in the participle form.

questions.prompt: ___ had she sat down than the phone rang.
questions.explanation: "No sooner ... than" is the fixed pair for one event immediately following another. "Hardly ... when" is the other.

questions.prompt: Not only ___ the deadline, but he also apologised badly.
questions.explanation: "Not only" at the front triggers inversion with the auxiliary "did", and the main verb returns to its base form.

questions.prompt: Only after the meeting ___ what had been decided.
questions.explanation: "Only" + a time phrase at the front inverts the subject and auxiliary.

questions.prompt: She speaks ___.
questions.explanation: English keeps the verb and its object together. An adverb of manner goes after the object, not between verb and object.

questions.prompt: We go to the cinema ___.
questions.explanation: Adverbs of frequency come before the time phrase, and in mid-position before the main verb in other patterns.

questions.prompt: ___ did the committee expect such a response.
questions.explanation: "Little" used as a negative adverb at the front means "not at all", and it takes inversion.

questions.prompt: So convincing ___ that nobody objected.
questions.explanation: When "so" + adjective is fronted for emphasis, the subject and verb invert.

topics.title: Prepositions of time and place
topics.summary: Prepositions rarely translate directly from another language, so they have to be learned as part of the phrase rather than as separate words.
points: Time: at a clock time, on a day or date, in a month, season or year.
Place: at a point, on a surface, in an enclosed space.
Transport: on a bus, train or plane; in a car or taxi.
Learn the whole phrase — "on Monday morning", "at the weekend" — not the preposition alone.

questions.prompt: The meeting is ___ Tuesday ___ 3 o'clock.
questions.explanation: Days take "on" and clock times take "at". This pairing covers most appointment sentences you will ever write.

questions.prompt: She was born ___ March 1998.
questions.explanation: Months and years take "in". You would only use "on" with a full date: on 5 March.

questions.prompt: I'll meet you ___ the bus stop.
questions.explanation: "At" treats a place as a point on a map rather than a space you go inside. Compare "in the shop".

questions.prompt: We travelled ___ car and then ___ the train.
questions.explanation: "By car" is the general method; once you name a specific vehicle you go "on the train" but "in the car".

questions.prompt: The keys are ___ the table.
questions.explanation: A table is a flat surface, so things sit "on" it. "In the table" would mean inside the wood.

questions.prompt: He works ___ night.
questions.explanation: "At night" is a fixed exception — compare "in the morning", "in the afternoon", "in the evening". It simply has to be memorised.

questions.prompt: The shop opens ___ the weekend.
questions.explanation: British English says "at the weekend"; American English says "on the weekend". IELTS accepts either, but stay consistent.

questions.prompt: Please hand it in ___ Friday at the latest.
questions.explanation: "By" means at or before that point — a deadline. "Until" would mean the action continues right up to Friday.

questions.prompt: The lecture starts ___ nine o'clock ___ Monday morning.
questions.explanation: "At" for clock times, "on" for days and dates. "In" is for longer stretches: months, seasons, years.

questions.prompt: She has lived in Leeds ___ 2019.
questions.explanation: "Since" marks the starting point. "For" would need a length of time: for five years.

questions.prompt: We waited ___ the bus stop ___ twenty minutes.
questions.explanation: "At" treats the bus stop as a point on a route. "For" introduces a duration.

questions.prompt: The keys are ___ the drawer, under the papers.
questions.explanation: "In" for something enclosed by the drawer. "On" would put them on its surface.

questions.prompt: I will finish the report ___ Friday at the latest.
questions.explanation: "By" means at or before that point. "Until" would mean the finishing continues right up to Friday.

questions.prompt: There is a chemist ___ the corner of the street.
questions.explanation: British usage puts a shop "on the corner". "In the corner" describes the inside angle of a room.

questions.prompt: He was born ___ the summer of 1998.
questions.explanation: "In" is used for seasons, months and years. "During" would be possible but changes the emphasis to the span.

questions.prompt: The painting hangs ___ the fireplace.
questions.explanation: "Above" means higher than, without touching. "On" would mean it rests against the fireplace itself.

topics.title: Countable and uncountable nouns
topics.summary: English decides for you which nouns can be counted, and its choices are not always logical. Getting this wrong affects the verb, the article and the quantifier all at once.
points: Uncountable nouns have no plural and take a singular verb: information, advice, furniture, luggage, research.
Use much / little / a great deal of with uncountables; many / few / a number of with countables.
"Some" and "a lot of" work with both.
To count an uncountable, add a unit: a piece of advice, two items of luggage.

questions.prompt: He gave me some useful ___.
questions.explanation: "Advice" is uncountable in English, so it has no plural and takes no "a". To count it, say "a piece of advice".

questions.prompt: There isn't ___ time left.
questions.explanation: "Time" here is uncountable, so it takes "much". "Many" only goes with things you can count individually.

questions.prompt: The ___ in this flat is very old.
questions.explanation: "Furniture" is uncountable and takes a singular verb — "is", not "are". The same is true of luggage and equipment.

questions.prompt: Only ___ students passed the exam.
questions.explanation: Students are countable, so "a few". "A little" would be right for an uncountable noun such as "a little water".

questions.prompt: Recent ___ suggests the opposite.
questions.explanation: "Research" is uncountable in English even though it is countable in many other languages — a very common IELTS error.

questions.prompt: Would you like ___ of tea?
questions.explanation: To count an uncountable noun, put a unit in front of it: a cup of tea, a slice of bread, a piece of information.

questions.prompt: ___ people were waiting outside.
questions.explanation: "People" is a plural countable noun, so it takes "a number of". "A great deal of" belongs with uncountables such as money or effort.

questions.prompt: We need to buy new ___.
questions.explanation: "Equipment" is uncountable. If you must count it, say "pieces of equipment" or name the items instead.

questions.prompt: Could you give me ___ information about the course?
questions.explanation: "Information" is uncountable in English, so it takes "some" rather than "a" or "a few".

questions.prompt: There ___ too much furniture in this room.
questions.explanation: "Furniture" is uncountable and takes a singular verb, even though it refers to many objects.

questions.prompt: How ___ luggage are you taking?
questions.explanation: "Much" goes with uncountable nouns. To count them you need a unit: how many suitcases.

questions.prompt: She gave me ___ advice that changed my mind.
questions.explanation: "Advice" is uncountable, so a single item needs a counter: a piece of advice.

questions.prompt: We have ___ chairs but not enough tables.
questions.explanation: "Plenty of" works with countable nouns like chairs. "Much" and "a great deal of" go with uncountables.

questions.prompt: I only have ___ money left.
questions.explanation: "Money" is uncountable, so the small quantity is "a little". "A few" would need coins or notes.

questions.prompt: ___ of the equipment was damaged in transit.
questions.explanation: "Equipment" is uncountable, so "some" fits. "A number of" and "many" require countable nouns.

questions.prompt: There is ___ evidence to support that claim.
questions.explanation: "Evidence" is uncountable, and "little" without "a" stresses that there is hardly any.

topics.title: Reported speech: tense shifts
topics.summary: When you report what someone said, the tense usually shifts one step back into the past, and time and place words change too. This is where a lot of writing and speaking errors come from.
points: Present tenses shift one step back: am/is/are → was/were, present perfect → past perfect.
Modals shift too: will → would, can → could, must (obligation) → had to.
Time and place words change: tomorrow → the next day, this → that, here → there.
Reported yes/no questions use "if" or "whether" and normal statement word order.

questions.prompt: She said, "I am tired." She said (that) she ___ tired.
questions.explanation: Present becomes past in reported speech after a past reporting verb ("said"). "Am" shifts back to "was".

questions.prompt: "I will call you," he said. He said he ___ call me.
questions.explanation: "Will" shifts to "would" in reported speech after a past reporting verb.

questions.prompt: "I have finished," she said. She said she ___ finished.
questions.explanation: Present perfect shifts to past perfect (had + past participle) in reported speech.

questions.prompt: "We are leaving now," they said. They said they ___ leaving then.
questions.explanation: Present continuous shifts to past continuous, and "now" also changes to "then".

questions.prompt: "I can swim," he said. He said he ___ swim.
questions.explanation: "Can" shifts to "could" in reported speech.

questions.prompt: "I must leave early," he said. He said he ___ leave early.
questions.explanation: "Must" expressing obligation usually shifts to "had to" in reported speech.

questions.prompt: "Don't touch that," she told him. She told him ___ touch that.
questions.explanation: A negative imperative reports as "told him not to" + infinitive.

questions.prompt: "Where do you live?" she asked me. She asked me where ___.
questions.explanation: Reported questions use statement word order, with no do/does/did, and the tense shifts back: "I lived".

questions.prompt: "Can you help me?" he asked. He asked ___ help him.
questions.explanation: Reported yes/no questions use "if" or "whether", and "can" shifts to "could".

questions.prompt: "I'll see you tomorrow," she said. She said she would see me ___.
questions.explanation: "Tomorrow", reported on a different day, becomes "the next day".

questions.prompt: "This is delicious," she said. Retelling the story later, he said she had said ___ was delicious.
questions.explanation: When retelling later, away from the original moment, "this" typically shifts to "that".

questions.prompt: He said, "I am going to buy a car." He said he ___ going to buy a car.
questions.explanation: "Am" shifts to "was" — the present tense moves one step back into the past.

questions.prompt: "I have never been to Spain," she said. She said she ___ never been to Spain.
questions.explanation: Present perfect shifts to past perfect: "had never been".

questions.prompt: "You should apologise," she told him. She told him he ___ apologise.
questions.explanation: "Should" stays the same in reported speech — it is already a distanced, hypothetical form.

questions.prompt: "I'm working on it now," he said. He said he ___ on it then.
questions.explanation: Present continuous becomes past continuous, and "now" becomes "then".

questions.prompt: "I had already eaten," she said. She said she ___ already eaten.
questions.explanation: Past perfect stays the same in reported speech — it is already the most "back" tense available.

topics.title: Subject–verb agreement with long subjects
topics.summary: The verb has to agree with its true subject, not with whatever noun happens to sit closest to it. Long subjects with phrases in the middle are where this goes wrong most often.
points: The verb agrees with the head noun of the subject, not with a noun in a phrase between them.
"Each", "every" and "neither" take a singular verb, even before something that looks plural.
"The number of" is singular; "a number of" is plural.
Collective nouns like team, family and government usually take a singular verb in careful written English.

questions.prompt: The list of items ___ on the table.
questions.explanation: The subject is "the list" (singular); "of items" only describes it. Ignore the noun inside the prepositional phrase.

questions.prompt: Each of the students ___ a laptop.
questions.explanation: "Each of" takes a singular verb, even though "students" is plural — "each" is the true subject.

questions.prompt: The number of accidents ___ fallen this year.
questions.explanation: "The number of" is treated as singular. Compare "a number of accidents have fallen", which is plural.

questions.prompt: A number of complaints ___ been received.
questions.explanation: "A number of" behaves as a plural quantifier and takes a plural verb.

questions.prompt: Neither of the answers ___ correct.
questions.explanation: "Neither of" takes a singular verb in careful written English, even though it refers to two things.

questions.prompt: The results of the survey ___ surprising.
questions.explanation: The head noun is "results" (plural); "of the survey" is just a modifier, so the verb must be plural.

questions.prompt: My family ___ planning a trip together.
questions.explanation: "Family" is a collective noun and takes a singular verb when treated as one unit, the standard choice in written English.

questions.prompt: The committee ___ meeting on Friday.
questions.explanation: In careful written English a collective noun like "committee" takes a singular verb when it acts as one body.

questions.prompt: Everyone in the room ___ aware of the risk.
questions.explanation: "Everyone" is always singular, whatever comes after it.

questions.prompt: The information in these reports ___ out of date.
questions.explanation: "Information" is uncountable and singular; "reports" sits inside a modifying phrase and does not control the verb.

questions.prompt: Neither the manager nor the assistants ___ available today.
questions.explanation: When a subject joined by "nor" has a plural noun closest to the verb, the verb agrees with that closer noun.

questions.prompt: Either the players or the coach ___ to blame.
questions.explanation: With "either… or", the verb agrees with the noun nearest to it — "the coach" (singular).

questions.prompt: The cost of the repairs ___ higher than expected.
questions.explanation: The subject is "the cost" (singular); "of the repairs" only describes which cost.

questions.prompt: A range of options ___ available to applicants.
questions.explanation: "A range of options" is treated as plural because attention is on the individual options, not the range itself.

questions.prompt: The police ___ investigating the incident.
questions.explanation: "Police" is always grammatically plural in English, unlike most collective nouns.

questions.prompt: One of the biggest problems ___ a lack of funding.
questions.explanation: "One" is the true subject and is singular; "of the biggest problems" only narrows down which one.

topics.title: Comparative and superlative structures
topics.summary: Comparing two things or picking out the top of a group follows fixed patterns based on how long the adjective is, plus a handful of irregular words to memorise.
points: One-syllable adjectives add -er/-est: tall, taller, tallest.
Adjectives ending consonant + y change y to i: happy, happier, happiest.
Adjectives of two or more syllables usually take more/most instead: more careful, most careful.
Comparing two things uses "than"; comparing three or more uses "the" + superlative.

questions.prompt: This bag is ___ than that one.
questions.explanation: One-syllable adjectives add -er to compare two things: heavy → heavier.

questions.prompt: She is ___ student in the class.
questions.explanation: Short adjectives take -est for the superlative, and the superlative needs "the" because it compares three or more.

questions.prompt: This exam was ___ than the last one.
questions.explanation: Adjectives of two or more syllables like "difficult" use "more" rather than an -er ending.

questions.prompt: He is ___ than his brother.
questions.explanation: One-syllable adjectives add -er, and comparing two people needs "than", not "the".

questions.prompt: This is ___ city I have ever visited.
questions.explanation: A superlative comparing this city with all others needs "the" plus "most" for a longer adjective.

questions.prompt: The weather today is ___ than yesterday.
questions.explanation: "Bad" has an irregular comparative: bad, worse, worst.

questions.prompt: This is by far ___ solution.
questions.explanation: "By far" signals a superlative — the strongest of all options — so it needs "the simplest".

questions.prompt: She runs ___ than I do.
questions.explanation: One-syllable adverbs add -er for comparisons between two.

questions.prompt: This laptop is ___ expensive as that one.
questions.explanation: Equal comparisons use "as + adjective + as", not "than".

questions.prompt: The city has become ___ crowded over the years.
questions.explanation: "Increasingly" is the adverb used before an adjective to show a gradual comparative change over time.

questions.prompt: This route is ___ than I expected.
questions.explanation: "Far" can strengthen a comparative: "far shorter" means much shorter. "Farer" is not a word.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: She is happiest now than before.
questions.explanation: "Happy" ends consonant + y, so the comparative is "happier" — never doubled with "more" as well.

questions.prompt: The more you practise, ___ you become.
questions.explanation: The double comparative pattern needs "the" in both halves: "The more..., the better...".

questions.prompt: This is one of ___ buildings in the city.
questions.explanation: "One of the + superlative + plural noun" is a fixed pattern for something among the top group.

questions.prompt: Her second novel was ___ than her first.
questions.explanation: "Good" has an irregular comparative: good, better, best.

questions.prompt: This model is slightly ___ than the previous one.
questions.explanation: "Efficient" has three syllables, so it takes "more" rather than an -er ending.

topics.title: Embedded and indirect questions
topics.summary: When a question sits inside a bigger sentence, it stops behaving like a question. The word order reverts to a normal statement, which trips up even confident speakers.
points: Inside a bigger sentence, a question loses its question word order: statement order returns.
Do not use do/does/did in an embedded question.
For yes/no questions, embed with "if" or "whether".
Keep the question mark only if the whole sentence is still a direct question.

questions.prompt: Could you tell me ___?
questions.explanation: Inside "could you tell me", the question reverts to statement order: subject before verb.

questions.prompt: I wonder ___ this seat is taken.
questions.explanation: A yes/no question embedded in a statement needs "if" or "whether", not the original question form.

questions.prompt: Do you know ___ he lives?
questions.explanation: The embedded question drops "does" and simply becomes "where he lives".

questions.prompt: I'm not sure ___ she is coming.
questions.explanation: "Whether" introduces an embedded yes/no question, just like "if".

questions.prompt: She asked me ___ I had finished.
questions.explanation: A reported yes/no question uses "if" plus statement word order: "if I had finished".

questions.prompt: Can you tell me ___ the museum opens?
questions.explanation: Statement word order returns inside the embedded question: "what time the museum opens".

questions.prompt: I have no idea ___.
questions.explanation: After "I have no idea", the clause follows statement order and keeps the present tense if the fact is still true.

questions.prompt: Nobody knows ___ the keys are.
questions.explanation: The embedded question needs statement order: "where the keys are", not "where are the keys".

questions.prompt: I'd like to know ___ this happened.
questions.explanation: "Why" plus statement order — "why this happened" — with no "did" inserted.

questions.prompt: Could you explain ___?
questions.explanation: Embedded questions never use "does"; the subject comes before the verb: "how it works".

questions.prompt: I'm curious ___ she said yes.
questions.explanation: "Why" introduces the embedded question directly, with statement order and no auxiliary "did".

questions.prompt: Let me know ___ you need any help.
questions.explanation: A yes/no embedded question needs "whether" (or "if").

questions.prompt: He couldn't remember ___ he had left his keys.
questions.explanation: The whole clause, including subject, auxiliary and verb, keeps statement order: "where he had left".

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: I don't know what does she want.
I don't know what she wants.
I don't know does she want what.
I don't know what she want.
questions.explanation: The embedded clause needs statement order and correct subject–verb agreement: "what she wants".

questions.prompt: I asked her ___ the report by Friday.
questions.explanation: A reported yes/no question needs "if" plus statement order.

questions.prompt: Can you tell me ___?
questions.explanation: The embedded question drops normal question inversion: "who that man is".

topics.title: Forming questions
topics.summary: Direct questions in English move a verb before the subject. Which verb moves — and whether "do" needs to be added — depends on what auxiliary is already there.
points: Yes/no questions move the auxiliary or "be" before the subject.
With no other auxiliary present in present or past simple, add do/does/did.
Question words go before the auxiliary: what, where, when, why, who, how.
Questions about the subject itself do not use do/does/did: "Who called you?"

questions.prompt: ___ you like tea?
questions.explanation: "You" in the present simple needs "do" as the auxiliary, since there is no other auxiliary verb.

questions.prompt: ___ she work in this building?
questions.explanation: "She" is third person singular, so the present simple auxiliary is "does".

questions.prompt: Which is correct?
questions.explanation: In a "be" question, "be" moves before the subject: "are you going".

questions.prompt: ___ called you last night?
questions.explanation: When the question word asks about the subject itself, no "did" is needed: "Who called you?"

questions.prompt: ___ did you buy that jacket?
questions.explanation: The question word "where" comes first, followed by the normal auxiliary "did" and the subject.

questions.prompt: Which is correct?
options: How many languages does she speak?
How many languages she does speak?
Does how many languages she speak?
questions.explanation: The auxiliary "does" comes right after the question phrase and before the subject.

questions.prompt: ___ you finished your homework yet?
questions.explanation: A present perfect question needs "have"/"has" before the subject, not "do".

questions.prompt: ___ is your favourite type of music?
questions.explanation: "What" asks about an open choice from an unlimited set; "which" is used when the options are limited or specified, such as choosing between two named types.

questions.prompt: ___ book is this — yours or mine?
questions.explanation: "Which" is used when the choice is between a limited, known set of options — here, two people.

questions.prompt: ___ car is parked outside?
questions.explanation: "Whose" asks about possession. "Who's" is a contraction of "who is" and means something different.

questions.prompt: ___ does this word mean?
questions.explanation: "What" asks for a definition or an open answer; "which" would suggest choosing from known options.

questions.prompt: Which question is correctly formed?
options: How many brothers do you have?
Do you have how many brothers?
questions.explanation: The question word phrase comes first, then the auxiliary "do", then the subject and main verb.

questions.prompt: ___ the shops close on Sundays?
questions.explanation: "The shops" is plural, so the present simple auxiliary is "do".

questions.prompt: ___ happened to your arm?
questions.explanation: When "what" is the subject of the question (what happened), no extra auxiliary is added.

questions.prompt: Which is correct?
options: Is she not is coming tonight?
questions.explanation: A negative question with "be" simply contracts "is" and "not" and moves the whole form before the subject.

questions.prompt: ___ long have you lived here?
questions.explanation: "How long" is the fixed question phrase for duration.

topics.title: Prepositions after common verbs
topics.summary: Many verbs are followed by a fixed preposition that does not translate logically from another language. The preposition can even change the meaning of the verb.
points: Many verbs are followed by a fixed preposition that has to be learned, not guessed.
The preposition can change the meaning: agree with a person, agree on a plan, agree to a proposal.
Learn the verb and its preposition together as one unit.
A preposition is always followed by a noun or -ing form, never a bare infinitive.

questions.prompt: She apologised ___ being late.
questions.explanation: "Apologise for" a thing you did wrong. "Apologise to" is used before the person you are apologising to.

questions.prompt: He is responsible ___ the whole project.
questions.explanation: "Responsible for" is the fixed pairing in English, even though other languages often use a different preposition here.

questions.prompt: The results depend ___ the weather.
questions.explanation: "Depend on" is fixed. "Depend of" and "depend from" do not exist in standard English.

questions.prompt: She's good ___ solving problems quickly.
questions.explanation: "Good at" is the fixed pairing for skills and abilities.

questions.prompt: We're looking forward ___ the results.
questions.explanation: "Look forward to" is fixed, and the "to" here is a preposition, so it is followed by -ing, not a bare verb.

questions.prompt: I don't agree ___ your explanation.
questions.explanation: "Agree with" a person or an idea. "Agree to" is used for a plan or proposal, and "agree on" for something decided jointly.

questions.prompt: They accused him ___ lying.
questions.explanation: "Accuse someone of" doing something is the fixed pattern.

questions.prompt: She succeeded ___ persuading them.
questions.explanation: "Succeed in" doing something is the standard pairing.

questions.prompt: He complained ___ the noise.
questions.explanation: "Complain about" a problem is standard. "Complain of" exists but is used mainly for symptoms of illness.

questions.prompt: The company invested heavily ___ new technology.
questions.explanation: "Invest in" something is the fixed collocation.

questions.prompt: I congratulated her ___ passing the exam.
questions.explanation: "Congratulate someone on" an achievement is fixed.

questions.prompt: She insisted ___ paying for dinner.
questions.explanation: "Insist on" is the fixed pairing in English; the verb that follows it must take the -ing form.

questions.prompt: We're relying ___ your support.
questions.explanation: "Rely on" is the fixed pairing in English; no other preposition follows this verb correctly.

questions.prompt: He is capable ___ great things.
questions.explanation: "Capable of" doing something is the fixed pairing.

questions.prompt: This project ___ several stages.
questions.explanation: "Consist of" means to be made up of parts. It is the only correct preposition here.

questions.prompt: They participated ___ the discussion.
questions.explanation: "Participate in" an activity is the fixed pairing.

topics.title: Talking about the future
topics.summary: English has no single future tense — the choice of form signals whether something is a plan, a spontaneous decision, a fixed arrangement or a timetable.
points: "Going to" for a plan already decided, or a prediction with present evidence.
"Will" for a decision made at the moment of speaking, an offer, or a general prediction.
Present continuous for a fixed future arrangement, usually with a time already set.
Present simple for a timetabled or scheduled event, like a train or a class.

questions.prompt: Look at those clouds! It ___ rain.
questions.explanation: "Going to" is used for a prediction based on present evidence — here, the clouds.

questions.prompt: I'm hungry. I think I ___ get a sandwich.
questions.explanation: "Will" expresses a decision made at the moment of speaking, not planned before.

questions.prompt: The train ___ at 9.15 tomorrow.
questions.explanation: Present simple is used for a fixed timetable, like a train, flight or class schedule.

questions.prompt: We ___ dinner with the Smiths on Saturday. It's already arranged.
questions.explanation: Present continuous describes a fixed arrangement with another person, already agreed and set in the diary.

questions.prompt: A: The phone's ringing. B: I ___ get it.
questions.explanation: "Will" is used for a spontaneous offer made at the moment of speaking.

questions.prompt: She's studied for months — I'm sure she ___ pass.
questions.explanation: "Will" is used here for a confident prediction based on general belief, not visible present evidence.

questions.prompt: I ___ the dentist at 10am tomorrow; I booked it last week.
questions.explanation: Present continuous is used for a personal appointment already fixed and booked, like this dentist visit.

questions.prompt: According to the plan, the new store ___ next month.
questions.explanation: "Going to" fits a plan that has already been decided, which is exactly what "according to the plan" signals.

questions.prompt: What time ___ the film start?
questions.explanation: Timetabled events like film showings use the present simple.

questions.prompt: Careful, that glass is right on the edge — it ___ fall!
questions.explanation: "Going to" is used for a prediction with visible evidence right now, like the glass on the edge.

questions.prompt: I promise I ___ call you as soon as I land.
questions.explanation: "Will" is used for promises made at the moment of speaking.

questions.prompt: This time next year, she ___ at university.
questions.explanation: The future continuous describes an action in progress at a specific point in the future.

questions.prompt: We ___ to the coast this weekend — the tickets are already booked.
questions.explanation: Present continuous is used for a fixed, already-arranged plan, shown here by the booked tickets.

questions.prompt: I think prices ___ rise again next year.
questions.explanation: "Will" is the natural choice for a general opinion or prediction about the future without present evidence.

questions.prompt: By 2030, most cars ___ electric.
questions.explanation: "Will" plus the base form is used for long-range predictions about the state of things.

questions.prompt: She's packed her bags — she ___ leave tonight.
questions.explanation: The packed bags are present evidence for a plan already decided, which calls for "going to".

topics.title: used to and would for past habits
topics.summary: Both describe repeated things from the past that no longer happen, but only one of them can describe a past state — the difference trips up even confident learners.
points: "Used to" describes a past habit or state that is no longer true.
"Would" also describes repeated past actions, but never a past state (never "would be", "would have").
Both need a base verb after them: used to live, would visit.
"Be used to" and "get used to" mean something completely different — being accustomed to something now.

questions.prompt: I ___ play football every weekend when I was younger.
questions.explanation: "Used to" + base verb describes a repeated past habit that has stopped.

questions.prompt: My grandfather ___ tell us stories by the fire every evening.
questions.explanation: "Would" can describe a repeated past action, just like "used to". Note it needs a base verb after it.

questions.prompt: There ___ be a cinema on this street, but it closed years ago.
questions.explanation: For a past state, not a repeated action, only "used to" works — "would" cannot describe a state like existence.

questions.prompt: She's lived in Berlin for years now, so she ___ the cold winters.
questions.explanation: "Be used to" means accustomed to something in the present — a completely different meaning from "used to do".

questions.prompt: It took him months to ___ working night shifts.
questions.explanation: "Get used to" means gradually become accustomed to something, and it takes -ing after it.

questions.prompt: We ___ go camping every summer as children.
questions.explanation: "Would" fits a repeated childhood activity, and it is the only correctly formed option here.

questions.prompt: I ___ hate vegetables, but now I love them.
questions.explanation: This describes a past state (hating vegetables) that has changed, so only "used to" works, not "would".

questions.prompt: When we were kids, we ___ walk to school together every day.
questions.explanation: "Would" describes a repeated past action.

questions.prompt: She ___ own a small bakery before she retired.
questions.explanation: Owning a bakery is a state, not a repeated action, so only "used to" is possible.

questions.prompt: After a few weeks, he ___ the noise of the city.
questions.explanation: "Got used to" describes the process of becoming accustomed, completed in the past.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: I would have a bike when I was young.
I used to have a bike when I was young.
I would used to have a bike.
I use to had a bike.
questions.explanation: Having a bike is a past state, so "used to" is required rather than "would".

questions.prompt: They ___ visit their grandparents every Sunday.
questions.explanation: "Would" fits a regularly repeated past visit.

questions.prompt: I'm still not ___ getting up this early.
questions.explanation: "Not used to" describes something you still find unfamiliar in the present.

questions.prompt: This town ___ be much quieter before the new road was built.
questions.explanation: Describing a general past state of the town calls for "used to", not "would".

questions.prompt: He ___ complain about the coffee every single morning.
questions.explanation: A repeated, habitual action in the past can be described with "would".

questions.prompt: Have you ___ living without a car yet?
questions.explanation: "Have you got used to" asks whether the process of adjustment is complete.

topics.title: Tag questions
topics.summary: A tag question checks or confirms information by adding a short question to the end of a statement. The tag always flips the polarity of the main clause.
points: A positive statement takes a negative tag; a negative statement takes a positive tag.
The tag repeats the auxiliary verb from the main clause, or adds do/does/did if there is none.
"I am" has the irregular tag "aren't I".
After "Let's", the tag is always "shall we".

questions.prompt: You're coming to the party, ___?
questions.explanation: A positive statement takes a negative tag, and the tag repeats "are" from "you're".

questions.prompt: She doesn't like coffee, ___?
questions.explanation: A negative statement takes a positive tag, matching the auxiliary "does".

questions.prompt: I'm right, ___?
questions.explanation: "Aren't I" is the standard irregular tag used after "I am" in a positive statement.

questions.prompt: Let's go for a walk, ___?
questions.explanation: "Let's" always takes the fixed tag "shall we", regardless of the rest of the sentence.

questions.prompt: They've finished the project, ___?
questions.explanation: The tag repeats the auxiliary "have" from the main clause, and turns negative because the statement is positive.

questions.prompt: He can't swim, ___?
questions.explanation: A negative statement takes a positive tag, repeating the modal "can".

questions.prompt: You didn't call her, ___?
questions.explanation: A negative statement takes a positive tag, matching the auxiliary "did".

questions.prompt: Close the door, ___?
questions.explanation: After an imperative, "will you" is the standard tag, used as a soft request.

questions.prompt: Nobody called, ___?
questions.explanation: "Nobody" is treated as negative, so it takes a positive tag: "did they".

questions.prompt: You'd rather stay home, ___?
questions.explanation: The tag repeats "'d" as "would", and since the statement is positive, the tag turns negative.

questions.prompt: There's a problem, ___?
questions.explanation: When the subject is "there", the tag must also use "there", not "it".

questions.prompt: She'll be here soon, ___?
questions.explanation: The tag repeats the auxiliary "will" and turns negative, since the statement is positive.

questions.prompt: Nothing went wrong, ___?
questions.explanation: "Nothing" counts as negative, so the tag is positive: "did it".

questions.prompt: You've never been to Rome, ___?
questions.explanation: "Never" makes the statement negative in meaning, so the tag is positive: "have you".

questions.prompt: We should leave now, ___?
questions.explanation: The tag repeats the modal "should" and turns negative, since the statement is positive.

questions.prompt: I don't need to sign here, ___?
questions.explanation: The tag repeats the auxiliary "do" from the negative statement and turns positive.

topics.title: -ing and -ed adjectives
topics.summary: These two adjective forms come from the same verb but describe opposite roles: one causes a feeling, the other experiences it. Mixing them up changes who is doing what to whom.
points: The -ing adjective describes the thing or person that causes the feeling: a boring film.
The -ed adjective describes the person who experiences the feeling: I was bored.
Never say "I am boring" to mean you feel bored — it means you cause boredom in others.
The same rule applies to interesting/interested, exciting/excited, confusing/confused, and many more pairs.

questions.prompt: The lecture was so ___ that half the class fell asleep.
questions.explanation: The lecture causes the feeling, so it takes the -ing form: "boring".

questions.prompt: I was really ___ by the ending of the film.
questions.explanation: The person experiencing the feeling takes the -ed form: "surprised".

questions.prompt: This is a very ___ result.
questions.explanation: The result causes confusion in the reader, so it takes the -ing form.

questions.prompt: After the long flight, everyone felt ___.
questions.explanation: The passengers experience tiredness, so the -ed form is needed: "exhausted".

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: I am boring of this job.
I am bored of this job.
questions.explanation: The person feels the boredom, so "bored" (-ed) is correct. "I am boring" would mean you cause boredom in others.

questions.prompt: The news was ___ — nobody could believe it.
questions.explanation: The news causes the shock, so it takes the -ing form.

questions.prompt: She felt ___ after reading the results.
questions.explanation: She experiences the feeling, so the -ed adjective is needed.

questions.prompt: It was a ___ experience — I'll never forget it.
questions.explanation: The experience causes fear, so it takes the -ing form.

questions.prompt: The children were ___ by the fireworks.
questions.explanation: The children experience amazement, so the -ed form fits.

questions.prompt: This puzzle is quite ___.
questions.explanation: The puzzle causes interest, so it takes the -ing form.

questions.prompt: I felt ___ when nobody replied to my message.
questions.explanation: The speaker experiences the feeling of annoyance, so the -ed form is correct.

questions.prompt: The match was extremely ___.
questions.explanation: The match causes excitement in the fans, so it takes the -ing form.

questions.prompt: He looked ___ when he heard the news.
questions.explanation: He is the person who feels worried, so the -ed form is correct.

questions.prompt: That was one of the most ___ books I've ever read.
questions.explanation: The book causes fascination in the reader, so it takes the -ing form.

questions.prompt: I'm ___ in how this machine works.
questions.explanation: The speaker feels interest, so the -ed form is needed here — "interested in" is also a fixed collocation.

questions.prompt: The traffic this morning was ___.
questions.explanation: The traffic causes frustration in drivers, so it takes the -ing form.
